message.content:
Let \(p=101\). For \(1\le m\le p-1\), define

\[
A_m=\sum_{r=1}^{m}2^{-\lfloor pr/m\rfloor}.
\]

For fixed \(m\),

\[
\left\lfloor \frac{p(k+m)}{m}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor \frac{pk}{m}\right\rfloor+p,
\]

so

\[
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}2^{-\lfloor pk/m\rfloor}
=
\sum_{r=1}^{m}\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}2^{-(\lfloor pr/m\rfloor+pt)}
=
\frac{A_m}{1-2^{-p}}.
\]

Thus the desired sum is

\[
S=\frac{1}{1-2^{-p}}\sum_{m=1}^{p-1}A_m.
\]

Now pair \(m\) with \(p-m\). For \(1\le m\le (p-1)/2\), consider the finite exponent lists

\[
L_m=\left\{\left\lfloor \frac{pr}{m}\right\rfloor:1\le r\le m\right\},
\qquad
L_{p-m}=\left\{\left\lfloor \frac{ps}{p-m}\right\rfloor:1\le s\le p-m\right\}.
\]

For a denominator \(d\), an integer \(n\) with \(1\le n\le p-1\) appears in the corresponding list iff

\[
\left[\frac{nd}{p},\frac{(n+1)d}{p}\right)
\]

contains an integer. Writing \(nd=pq+a\) with \(1\le a\le p-1\), this happens iff \(a+d>p\).

For the pair \(m,p-m\), let \(a\) be the least positive residue of \(nm\pmod p\). Then the residue of \(n(p-m)\pmod p\) is \(p-a\). Hence \(n\) appears in \(L_m\) iff \(a+m>p\), and in \(L_{p-m}\) iff \(a+m<p\). For \(1\le n\le p-2\), equality \(a+m=p\) is impossible because it would imply \((n+1)m\equiv0\pmod p\), contradicting the primality of \(p\). So each \(n=1,2,\dots,p-2\) appears exactly once among the two lists. The exponent \(p-1\) appears in neither, while \(p\) appears in both.

Therefore

\[
A_m+A_{p-m}
=
\sum_{n=1}^{p-2}2^{-n}+2\cdot 2^{-p}
=
1-2^{-(p-1)}.
\]

With \(p=101\), there are \(50\) such pairs, so

\[
\sum_{m=1}^{100}A_m=50(1-2^{-100}).
\]

Hence

\[
S
=
\frac{50(1-2^{-100})}{1-2^{-101}}
=
\frac{100(2^{100}-1)}{2^{101}-1}.
\]

\[
\boxed{\frac{100(2^{100}-1)}{2^{101}-1}}
\]
